title: Composition Patterns
summary: **Composition** is React's primary way to reuse and combine UI: components accept other components via the `children` prop and slots instead of inheriting behavior, which keeps components flexible and decoupled.

subtopics.title: The children prop
subtopics.explanation: Anything nested between a component's JSX tags is automatically passed to it as the special children prop. The component decides where that content appears by rendering {children}, which lets a generic wrapper like Card stay unaware of what it contains. The most common beginner bug is forgetting to actually render {children}, so the nested content silently disappears.

subtopics.title: Composition over inheritance
subtopics.explanation: React reuses and customizes UI by combining small components rather than subclassing a base component. This avoids the deep, rigid hierarchies that class inheritance creates and keeps each component focused and decoupled — the React docs explicitly recommend it. To share stateful logic without inheritance, you extract a custom hook rather than a base class.

subtopics.title: Specialization
subtopics.explanation: Specialization is building a specific component by configuring or wrapping a more generic one, rather than creating a subclass. A WelcomeDialog is just a Dialog with particular props; an IconButton is just a Button with an icon child. This keeps the generic component reusable while specific variants stay thin and declarative.

subtopics.title: Slots (named content props)
subtopics.explanation: When a component needs multiple independently-filled regions, you expose each as its own prop that accepts a React node — a 'slot'. A Dialog with title, body, and actions slots lets the parent control each region while the Dialog owns structure and styling. Rendering each slot conditionally (slot && ...) avoids stray dividers or padding when a region is empty.

subtopics.title: Composition vs configuration
subtopics.explanation: Configuration props customize a component with flat values and flags (variant, size, showHeader); composition props inject actual UI (children, slots). Configuration suits closed, fixed option sets, while composition wins for open-ended or structural variability that flags can't express. The warning sign to switch is 'prop explosion' — a component accumulating many boolean/variant props becomes unreadable and brittle.

subtopics.title: Container vs presentational
subtopics.explanation: This pattern splits components by responsibility: container components fetch data and hold state, while presentational components receive everything via props and just render markup. The separation makes presentational components trivially testable without data and lets the two layers change independently. With hooks, the 'container' role is often a custom hook rather than a wrapper component.

subtopics.title: children as elements and stable references
subtopics.explanation: Because children is just a prop holding already-created React elements, a parent can re-render due to its own state change without forcing those children to re-render — the children reference passed in stays stable. This 'pass children through' pattern is a lightweight performance win that avoids recreating subtrees inline. It only holds when the children are passed in from above rather than constructed in the re-rendering component's body.

subtopics.title: Render props (children as a function)
subtopics.explanation: children doesn't have to be markup — it can be a function the component calls with data, giving the parent control over how to render shared logic. This 'render prop' pattern was the classic pre-hooks way to share stateful behavior while inverting control of the output. Today custom hooks usually replace it, but you'll still encounter it in libraries and it remains a valid composition tool.

foundations.overview: React favors composition over inheritance. Instead of subclassing a component to change its behavior, you build small components and combine them — passing UI into a component through its children prop or through named slot props. This lets a generic component like Card or Modal stay unaware of what it contains while a parent supplies the specific content.
foundations.formalDefinition: Composition is the practice of building components by nesting and combining other components and passing renderable content (React nodes) as props — most commonly the special children prop, or additional named props for multiple 'slots' — rather than extending a base component class.
foundations.whyItMatters: Composition is how you achieve reuse without tight coupling. It avoids the fragile, deep hierarchies that inheritance creates and keeps each component focused on one job, which is why the React docs explicitly recommend it over inheritance.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a component as a picture frame with empty holes (slots). The frame defines structure and styling; the parent decides what photos go in each hole. The frame never needs to know about the photos, and any photo fits any frame.
foundations.browserPerspective: Composed components still produce one combined React element tree that reconciles into DOM as usual. children is just a prop holding React elements; React renders them wherever the parent places {children} in its JSX, so the final DOM reflects the nesting you wrote.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Layout wrappers (Card, Panel, PageLayout), modals and dialogs, buttons that wrap arbitrary labels/icons, list components that accept item renderers, and design-system primitives all rely on composition and slots.
foundations.businessImpact: Composable components form the backbone of design systems. They let teams ship consistent UI fast and adapt to new requirements by recombining existing parts instead of rewriting, which speeds delivery and reduces UI bugs.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Composition keeps components decoupled and testable: a presentational Card can be tested without any data, and a container can be tested without markup. It also avoids the brittle base-class hierarchies that make refactors risky.
foundations.performanceImpact: Passing children as elements means React can sometimes skip re-rendering those children when only the parent's own state changes (the children prop reference is stable), which can reduce wasted renders compared to inlining everything.
commonUseCases: Generic containers (Card, Panel, Modal) that wrap arbitrary content
Named slots like header/body/footer or icon/label
Specialized components built by configuring a generic one
Splitting data-fetching containers from presentational views

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should use class inheritance to share behavior between components.
commonMisconceptions.reality: React recommends composition; inheritance is almost never needed. Share logic via composition, props, or custom hooks instead.

commonMisconceptions.myth: children can only be text or a single element.
commonMisconceptions.reality: children can be any renderable node — text, one element, an array of elements, fragments, or even a function (render prop).

commonMisconceptions.myth: More configuration props always beats composition.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Past a few options, a pile of boolean/variant props becomes unreadable; exposing slots via children is often clearer and more flexible.

visualExplorer.title: Composition builds a tree
visualExplorer.caption: Composition is just nesting components into a tree — a parent passes content down through children/slots. Click nodes to see how a parent's render cascades to what it composes.

interactiveExamples.title: The children prop
interactiveExamples.explanation: A generic Card renders whatever you nest inside it via props.children. The Card owns the box/border; the parent owns the content.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A bordered card containing the heading and paragraph passed as children.

interactiveExamples.title: Named slots via props
interactiveExamples.explanation: When a component needs multiple regions, pass each as its own prop (a slot). Here Dialog has title, body, and actions slots so the parent controls each region independently.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A dialog with a titled header, a body region, and a footer of action buttons, each filled from a slot prop.

codeLab.title: Build a Card with header / body / footer slots
codeLab.instructions: Create a reusable Card that renders three named slots: header, children (body), and footer. The Card owns the border, spacing, and dividers; the parent supplies the content for each region. Render a Card in App showing a title in the header, text in the body, and a button in the footer.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A card with a bold header, body text, and a footer button, each region filled by the parent via slots.
hints: header and footer are slot props; body content comes through children.
Render each slot only when provided (header && ...) so empty regions don't show dividers.
Keep all structure/styling inside Card; the parent passes only content.

debuggingLab.title: The slot content vanishes
debuggingLab.symptom: The Card renders its border but the content passed inside the tags never appears.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Anything nested between a component's tags is passed as the children prop, but the component must actually render it. Card never references props.children, so React drops the nested content and only the empty wrapper appears.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to render {children} (or {props.children}) inside the component.
Naming a slot prop and then never placing it in the JSX.
Assuming nested JSX shows up automatically without being rendered.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Destructure children and render it inside the Card's wrapper div.

theory.question: What does 'composition over inheritance' mean in React, and how is it implemented?
theory.directAnswer: It means you reuse and customize components by combining them — passing content in through props like children — rather than extending a base component class. In practice you nest components and read props.children (or named slot props) so a generic component can wrap arbitrary content without knowing what it is.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A design principle: build flexible UI by assembling small components instead of creating subclasses of a base component.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Inheritance hierarchies in UI become deep, rigid, and hard to refactor. Composition keeps components decoupled and recombinable, which the React docs explicitly favor.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Content nested inside a component's JSX tags becomes its children prop; the component renders {children} wherever it wants. Multiple regions are exposed as additional named props (slots).

theory.whyImportant: It's a foundational React philosophy that interviewers use to check whether you think in components and props rather than class hierarchies.
theory.realWorldExample: A design-system Button wraps {children} so it can hold text, an icon, or both without separate IconButton/TextButton subclasses.

nestedTopics.title: children prop
nestedTopics.explanation: The special prop holding whatever is nested between a component's tags; render it with {children}.

nestedTopics.title: Specialization
nestedTopics.explanation: Building a specific component (e.g. WelcomeDialog) by composing/configuring a generic one (Dialog) rather than subclassing it.

nestedTopics.title: Slots
nestedTopics.explanation: Exposing multiple content regions as named props so a parent fills each independently.

followUps.question: When would inheritance ever be appropriate in React?
followUps.answer: Essentially never for components; the docs say no use cases warrant a component hierarchy. Share non-UI logic via custom hooks or plain functions instead.

followUps.question: How do you reuse stateful logic without inheritance?
followUps.answer: Extract it into a custom hook, which composes logic into any component without changing its UI structure.

theory.question: Compare composition props with configuration props. When does composition win?
theory.directAnswer: Configuration props customize a component with flat values and flags (variant, size, showHeader). Composition props pass in actual UI (children, slots). Composition wins when the variability is structural or open-ended — when a parent needs to control arbitrary content or layout — because a growing list of config flags becomes unreadable and can't express custom markup.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to make a component flexible: by toggling predefined options versus by injecting content.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Some flexibility is closed (a fixed set of variants) and suits config props; some is open (any content) and suits composition.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Config props branch internally on values; composition props render whatever node the parent supplies, so the component doesn't need to anticipate every case.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right axis of flexibility keeps APIs clean and is a frequent design-discussion question for component libraries.
theory.realWorldExample: A Modal exposes size as a config prop but title/body/footer as slots, because content is open-ended while size is a small fixed set.

nestedTopics.title: Prop explosion
nestedTopics.explanation: When too many boolean/variant props accumulate, the API becomes confusing — a sign to switch to slots.

nestedTopics.title: Inversion of control
nestedTopics.explanation: Composition hands control of content/layout back to the parent, making the component simpler and more reusable.

followUps.question: Can you mix both in one component?
followUps.answer: Yes — use config props for closed sets (size, variant) and composition/slots for open content; most real components do both.

scenario.question: A teammate built a Card that has grown to 15 boolean/variant props (showHeader, headerColor, hasFooter, footerAlign...). It's hard to use and keeps gaining props. How would you redesign it?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd convert it from a heavily configured component into a composable one with slots. Instead of flags describing the header, expose a header slot (and footer slot, with children as the body) so the parent passes the actual markup. That collapses the prop explosion, removes internal branching, and makes the Card open to cases it never anticipated.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A refactor from configuration-heavy API to a composition/slots API to stop prop explosion.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Trying to anticipate every variation with flags leads to an unmaintainable surface; composition hands content control to the caller.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Replace flags like showHeader/headerColor with a header prop that takes a React node; render it when present. The parent styles and structures its own header content.

scenario.whyImportant: Recognizing and fixing prop explosion is a practical, senior-leaning design skill for component libraries.

nestedTopics.title: Slots over flags
nestedTopics.explanation: Passing content via named props removes the need for many describing-the-content booleans.

nestedTopics.title: Container/presentational split
nestedTopics.explanation: Keeping Card presentational and pushing decisions to the caller reduces its responsibilities.

followUps.question: What do you lose by switching to slots?
followUps.answer: Some guardrails — callers can pass inconsistent markup. You can mitigate with subcomponents (Card.Header) or typed slot props for guidance.

coding.question: Implement a reusable Panel component with header and footer slots plus a body via children, rendering nothing for absent slots.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll destructure header, children, and footer. The Panel owns structure and dividers; each slot renders only when provided so empty regions don't show stray borders. children is the body. This keeps Panel generic and lets any parent supply content.
coding.lineByLine: Panel destructures three slots. The header and footer use short-circuit (header && ...) so they render only when passed, avoiding empty bordered regions. children is rendered in the middle as the body. App composes Panel by passing a header string, footer button node, and body children — Panel stays unaware of the specifics.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — render cost is proportional to the supplied content, not any loop.

alternativeApproaches.title: Compound components (Panel.Header / Panel.Footer)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Attach subcomponents to Panel so usage reads as nested JSX (<Panel><Panel.Header>...) which can be more discoverable than slot props.

alternativeApproaches.title: Single children with structural convention
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Pass everything as children and let the parent arrange it, trading guardrails for maximum flexibility.

followUps.question: How would you let callers style the body region?
followUps.answer: Accept a className/style prop or a bodyProps slot, or expose a compound Panel.Body subcomponent they fully control.

systemDesign.question: Design the API for a reusable, accessible DataTable used across many teams: sorting, pagination, row selection, custom cell rendering, and large datasets. What does the public API look like, and how do you stay flexible without becoming a config monster?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Favor composition over a giant props object. Ship a headless core (a useTable hook) that owns sort/page/selection state and returns state + handlers, while consumers render markup. For out-of-the-box UI, provide compound components (<DataTable><DataTable.Column/>) so columns are declared as JSX and cells use a render function — teams customize by composing, not by adding new props. Make state controllable (controlled sort/page/selection with onChange) so server-side data and virtualization plug in, and virtualize rows for large sets. Accessibility is built in: native table semantics, aria-sort on headers, keyboard navigation, labeled selection checkboxes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered table: a headless state hook plus an optional compound-component UI, with controllable state and column-driven rendering.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single mega-props table becomes an unmaintainable config monster; teams need to override rendering and plug in server data without forking the component.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: useTable manages sort/page/selection and exposes state+handlers; compound components read it via context; render props customize cells; controlled props let a parent drive state for server-side operations; a virtualizer windows the rows.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Design-system tables are asked constantly: they test API design, composition vs configuration, controlled/uncontrolled patterns, accessibility, and performance at once.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: TanStack Table popularized the headless approach; MUI/AntD tables show the compound + controlled pattern.

nestedTopics.title: Composition over configuration
nestedTopics.explanation: Declare columns as JSX and pass cell renderers as functions instead of adding a new boolean prop for every variation.

nestedTopics.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled
nestedTopics.explanation: Support both: uncontrolled for quick use; controlled (value + onChange) so server-side sorting/pagination and external state can drive the table.

nestedTopics.title: Accessibility & virtualization
nestedTopics.explanation: Native <table> semantics + aria-sort + keyboard nav, and window the rows so 100k rows don't mount 100k nodes.

followUps.question: Client-side vs server-side sorting/pagination — how does the API change?
followUps.answer: Make those operations controlled: the table emits onSortChange/onPageChange and renders whatever rows it's given, so the parent can fetch a server page instead of slicing locally.

followUps.question: How do you keep row selection fast on 50k rows?
followUps.answer: Store selection as a Set/Map of ids (O(1) lookups), virtualize rows, and keep callback identities stable so memoized rows don't re-render.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Build a small set of composable primitives (Box, Card, Stack, Modal) that accept children and slots, then compose feature UI from them. Separate container components (data, state) from presentational components (markup driven by props) so each layer changes independently.
productionDeepDive.performance: Passing children as elements gives a stable prop reference, so a parent whose own state changes can re-render without forcing children to re-render (when children are passed through rather than created inline). Combine with memoization for hot paths.
productionDeepDive.security: Composed content is still rendered as React nodes, which escape text by default; the risk is only when you bypass that with dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Treat any slot that injects raw HTML as untrusted and sanitize it.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As a design system grows, composition keeps the component count manageable — new screens recombine existing primitives instead of adding bespoke variants. Establish slot conventions (header/body/footer) so components feel consistent.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Composition avoids brittle inheritance chains; each component has one responsibility and is testable in isolation. Prefer slots over ever-growing config flags to keep APIs readable.
productionDeepDive.observability: React DevTools shows the composed tree, making it easy to see which component owns which content and to spot unnecessary nesting or re-renders.

caseStudies.problem: A Card component accumulated dozens of config props to cover every layout variant and became unusable.
caseStudies.solution: Refactored to header/body/footer slots (and compound subcomponents), letting product teams compose the exact layout they needed.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Fewer guardrails on content vs. far simpler, more flexible API.
caseStudies.lessons: When variability is open-ended, expose slots rather than trying to enumerate every case with props.

keyTakeaways: React favors composition over inheritance: reuse components by combining them, not by subclassing.
Content nested in a component's tags arrives as the children prop; render it with {children}.
Expose multiple regions as named slot props (header/body/footer) so a parent fills each independently.
Use configuration props for closed option sets and composition/slots for open-ended content to avoid prop explosion.
Separate container (data/state) from presentational (markup) components to keep each decoupled and testable.
